rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing late compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, with substantial resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure slope sensitivity.
Reduce the gradient by one grid step to shorten elution while retaining the maximum CRF. The first pair is slope-sensitive but its current resolution of 2.46 leaves room to test this faster gradient.

The 4-minute gradient still achieves maximum CRF, but the first pair is close to the resolution threshold. Test higher temperature at the same slope to shorten retention and determine whether temperature improves that critical pair before attempting a 2-minute gradient.

Higher temperature harmed the critical first pair, so test the low-temperature limit at the same gradient slope. Improved selectivity could provide enough resolution margin to shorten or narrow the gradient next.

Test a 2-minute gradient at the temperature that best separates the critical pair, narrowing the solvent window to moderate the increase in steepness. The final peak may enter the hold, but the high final organic fraction should keep elution prompt.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward one step while preserving gradient slope and the favorable low temperature. This should accelerate the last peak; the key test is whether the first pair retains its narrow resolution margin.

Shift the window upward another step at unchanged slope to accelerate the last peak and reduce its hold-phase retention. The previous shift preserved first-pair resolution, so test whether that remains true as the early peaks approach the solvent front.
Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while slightly reducing gradient steepness. Check whether the early pair remains resolved as it moves closer to the solvent front.

Use the improved first-pair resolution margin to test a 5 °C temperature increase, shortening late retention without raising the starting organic fraction further. This probes whether maximum CRF can be maintained in a faster run.

Test whether a narrower gradient window can further shorten the fully resolved method, returning to 25 °C to favor first-pair selectivity. This deliberately probes the starting-organic boundary, where early-peak compression may outweigh the benefit of a shallower slope.

Keep the starting fraction below the early-peak compression boundary and reduce the final fraction to make the gradient shallower. Test whether that resolution gain offsets a further temperature increase while keeping all six peaks promptly eluted.

Move the first pair away from the solvent front while preserving the gradient slope of injection 10, the fastest fully resolved run so far. This tests whether a lower starting fraction provides more resolution margin at 30 °C with only a small retention-time cost.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method by lowering only the final organic fraction one step. The shallower gradient may improve the critical pair’s resolution margin while adding little to the last peak’s retention time.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to establish its speed–resolution boundary directly. First-pair resolution may fall below 1.5; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed method achieving the maximum CRF.

The faster temperature step lost resolution, so return to 25 °C and test a slightly shallower gradient for greater first-pair margin. This seeks a more robust maximum-CRF alternative with only a modest time cost relative to injection 10.

Test whether a shallower gradient and lower starting organic fraction restore first-pair resolution at 35 °C by keeping the early peaks away from the solvent front. The maximum CRF is already secured; this explores an alternative temperature–gradient balance without repeating a method.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step to make the gradient shallower and try to lift the critical pair from R = 1.42 above 1.5. The last peak will likely spend longer in the hold, but the preceding run suggests ample room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Injection 18 still flags the critical pair below threshold despite its rounded CRF, so lower temperature to improve selectivity and restore phi1 to 0.85 for faster late elution. This should provide a clearer resolution margin in a roughly 3-minute separation.

Lower temperature one step from injection 13 to improve first-pair selectivity while retaining rapid late elution. This tests a maximum-CRF alternative with more early retention than injection 16 and potentially better resolution margin than injection 8.

Reduce phi1 one step from injection 20 to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while keeping the early peaks clear of the solvent front. This should retain maximum CRF with a modest increase in late-peak retention; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 21 to test whether the narrower window shortens late elution while preserving its resolution margin. This refines a fully resolved region; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed method with maximum CRF.

Raise temperature one step from injection 22 to shorten hold-phase elution, using its first-pair resolution margin of 1.90. This should preserve maximum CRF while refining the faster end of this narrower-window method.

Test the remaining lower-phi0 neighbor of injection 10, the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. This keeps late elution fast while checking whether moving the early pair away from the solvent front compensates for the steeper gradient; its resolution may be marginal.

Use the final injection to test a shallower gradient for additional first-pair resolution margin, with late elution expected to remain comfortably below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
